recent_posts.title: Can 10 points always be covered by disjoint unit discs
recent_posts.summary: A geometry puzzle asks whether 10 arbitrary points on a 2D plane can always be covered by non-overlapping (disjoint) unit discs of radius 1. The challenge is to prove or disprove that such a covering is always possible regardless of point placement.

recent_posts.title: The mathematics behind Escher's recursive Print Gallery lithograph
recent_posts.summary: MC Escher's 1956 lithograph 'Print Gallery' is explored through a mathematical lens. The piece depicts a man viewing a painting that recursively contains the gallery itself. In 2003, mathematicians De Smit and Lenstra analyzed the underlying structure, revealing that the image is essentially a logarithmic transformation of itself. This analysis also answers what belongs in the mysterious blank spot at the center — a point where all spatial ambiguity in the recursive scene converges.

recent_posts.title: The subset sum puzzle
recent_posts.summary: A mathematical puzzle about subset sums: given 10 numbers chosen from 1 to 100, can you always find two distinct subsets with the same sum, or can the chooser pick numbers to prevent this? The puzzle asks which player has the winning strategy, with the solution to be revealed later as part of a monthly MoMath collaboration series.

recent_posts.title: Escher's most mathematically interesting piece
recent_posts.summary: A deep mathematical exploration of M.C. Escher's 1956 lithograph 'Print Gallery', revealing the complex analysis behind its self-referential loop. The piece walks through how Escher intuitively constructed a conformal mesh warp using a Droste-effect self-similar image, then reframes the same construction using complex logarithms and exponentials. Taking the log of a Droste image produces a doubly periodic tiling; rotating and scaling in log-space, then exponentiating, recreates Escher's warped loop as a complex power function. The blank center of the original piece is explained as a natural consequence of the spiral structure. The analysis connects to elliptic functions and modern number theory, showing that Escher's aesthetic intuitions unknowingly touched research-level mathematics.

recent_posts.title: Bacteria Grid Puzzle Solution
recent_posts.summary: A bacteria replication puzzle on a grid asks for the minimum moves to clear all 16 lattice points inside a box, starting from a single cell at the origin. The key insight is finding an invariant: a weighted sum assigned to each diagonal line (each line having half the weight of the previous) that never changes regardless of moves made. Since the total weight of the entire infinite grid sums to only 4, and the 16-point box already accounts for over 3.5 of that weight, the remaining weight outside the box is less than 1 — making it mathematically impossible for bacteria to ever fully escape the box. The puzzle's answer is that clearing the 4×4 box is impossible, and even the 3×3 box cannot be cleared for the same reason.

recent_posts.title: Deriving the volume formula for n-dimensional balls
recent_posts.summary: A lecture-style exploration of the formula for the volume of an n-dimensional ball. Starting from intuitive probability puzzles (what's the chance that x²+y² ≤ 1 for random x,y?), it builds up to the general formula V_n = π^(n/2) / (n/2)! · r^n. Key ideas include: the relationship between a ball's volume and its surface area via derivatives/integrals, an Archimedean projection argument generalized to higher dimensions via a 'knight's move' recurrence, the gamma function extending factorials to half-integers, and the surprising fact that unit ball volumes peak around 5 dimensions and then shrink toward zero in higher dimensions — a counterintuitive result relevant to machine learning, cryptography, and quantum mechanics.

recent_posts.title: The lattice bacteria puzzle
recent_posts.summary: A mathematical puzzle involving bacteria on a grid where cells replicate by moving one space up and one space right, leaving their original position empty. The challenge is to find the minimum number of moves needed to clear a 4×4 box starting from a single cell at the origin, with the constraint that only one cell can occupy each grid point.

recent_posts.title: Solution to the ladybug clock puzzle
recent_posts.summary: A ladybug puzzle solution reveals a counterintuitive result: when a ladybug randomly walks around a clock face coloring numbers, each position (1-11) has equal probability (1/11) of being the last colored. The key insight transforms the problem by waiting until the ladybug reaches a neighbor of any target number, then recognizing this becomes equivalent to a random walk question that's identical for all positions.

recent_posts.title: The ladybug clock puzzle
recent_posts.summary: A mathematical puzzle involving a ladybug performing a random walk on a clock face. Starting at 12, the ladybug moves randomly to neighboring numbers each second until all positions are visited. The challenge is to calculate the probability that position 6 is the last number to be colored. This is part of a monthly puzzle series in collaboration with mathematician Peter Winkler and MoMath Museum.
